items.title: Beyond intensity: pain distribution shapes healthcare- and treatment-seeking beliefs in individuals with and without clinical pain.
items.abstract: Pain is commonly described in sensory terms, yet its spatial characteristics are rarely quantified. We investigated whether lay beliefs about pain distribution influence theoretical decisions to seek care and treatment preferences. In a cross-sectional survey (N = 503; 49% reporting pain), participants completed thought experiments in which both visually presented pain distribution patterns (small, moderate, or large) and pain intensity (Numerical Rating Scale scores: 2, 5, 8/10) were systematically varied. For each scenario, they rated the likelihood of (1) seeking professional help (LoSH) and (2) taking analgesic medication (LoTM) on 0 to 100 scale. Participants also completed a spatial-intensity trade-off task, in which they chose between a fixed 20% reduction in intensity and variable reductions in pain distribution (20%-80%). A reversed version contrasted a fixed 80% reduction in pain distribution with variable reductions in pain intensity. LoSH and LoTM increased significantly with greater pain distribution (P < 0.001), mirroring the gradient observed for pain intensity. In the spatial-intensity trade-off task, participants' choice followed a sigmoid-like function (P < 0.001): 1% reduction in intensity was treated as equivalent to approximately a 3% reduction in distribution, indicating a systematic valuation of pain distribution. This ratio was lower in individuals experiencing pain compared with pain-free individuals. Moreover, 61% reported that pain distribution should be routinely considered in pain management alongside intensity. Results suggest that pain distribution is not merely a trivial descriptor, but a meaningful determinant of healthcare-related decision-making beliefs. Incorporating spatial metrics into clinical assessment and research may better capture how individuals implicitly evaluate pain severity.

items.title: Cannabinoid actions in a nonsurgical mouse model of sensitized dural nociceptors.
items.abstract: Cannabinoid 1 and 2 receptor (CB1R and CB2R) agonists alleviate inflammatory and neuropathic pain symptoms. However, central nervous system (CNS) side effects mediated by CB1Rs limit their widespread use. We developed peripherally restricted cannabinoids (PRCBs), which exhibit analgesic efficacy with minimal CNS side effects. Here, we examined PRCB actions in a mouse model of dural acid-induced hypersensitivity. Supradural injections of pH-6.0 (but not pH-7.4) saline (4.5 µL) in five-week-old female C57BL/6J mice induced periorbital allodynia (assessed with von Frey filaments) with recovery by 48 hours. By 72 hours, allodynia was elicited with a supradural pH-7.0 saline injection in pH-6.0 (but not pH-7.4) mice. The CB1R/CB2R agonist PRCB, 4-{2-[(1E)-1-[(4-propylnaphthalen-1-yl) methylidene]-1H-inden-3-yl]ethyl}morpholine (PrNMI) (5 µM) or the selective CB1R agonist arachidonyl-2'-chloroethylamide (ACEA, 5 µM), coapplied with pH-6.0 saline, prevented both the initial and latent allodynia, but coadministering pH 6.0 with the CB2R-selective agonist RNB61 (5 µM) did not. Coadministering pH-6.0/PrNMI with CB1R- or CB2R-selective inverse agonists abolished the preventative effects of PrNMI. Supradural pH-6.0 saline-evoked allodynia followed 72 hours later by coadministration of pH 7.0/PrNMI did not prevent latent allodynia. Patch recordings obtained from dural trigeminal ganglion neurons (dTGNs) acutely isolated from FluoroGold/pH-6.0 (but not pH-7.4)-injected mice had larger acid-induced depolarizations. All dTGNs had electrophysiological properties of Aδ- or C-type nociceptors. PrNMI (1 µM) suppressed acid-induced depolarizations in dTGNs from pH-7.4 (but not pH-6.0)-treated mice, whereas RNB61 (0.5 µM) had no effect. These findings indicate that PrNMI prevents acid-induced sensitization by coactivating neuronal CB1Rs and non-neuronal CB2Rs. Cannabinoid 2 receptor activation alone is insufficient, and once sensitized, combined CB1R/CB2R activation loses efficacy.

items.title: Distinct connectivity patterns subserve 2 dimensions of the chronic pain experience.
items.abstract: Identifying the neural correlates of chronic pain and their relationship to clinically relevant measures of disease has proven challenging due to high variability in individual patterns of functional brain connectivity and the rarity of ecologically valid scanning paradigms. Here, we address these limitations using data from the Multidisciplinary Approach to the Study of Pelvic Pain Symptom Patterns Study, which recruited a large sample of urologic chronic pain patients (n = 382) imaged repeatedly (range = 2-4) over 36 months. Intrinsic brain connectivity was recorded before and after a naturalistic challenge designed to elicit symptomatic pain and discomfort. Linear mixed-effects models revealed 2 neuroanatomically distinct patterns: pain at the time of scan was linked to connectivity within sensory-discriminative regions, while past-week recalled pain was associated with distributed patterns across regions implicated in memory, salience, and affective processing. These findings emphasize the dynamic roles of brain regions for different aspects of chronic pain.

items.title: Clinical and preclinical investigation of the mechanism promoting aura in post-traumatic headache and inhibition of pain-related behavior in mice by onabotulinumtoxinA.
items.abstract: Post-traumatic headache (PTH) is the most common consequence of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) and often resembles migraine. In 20% to 30% of migraine patients, headaches are preceded by aura, transient visual or sensory disturbances, which are caused by cortical spreading depression (CSD) that can induce headache pain. However, whether mTBI promotes the development of aura and CSD and their possible contributions to PTH remains unclear. We examined the incidence of new-onset aura in individuals with PTH who had no history of aura. Thirty-two percent (35/108) developed new aura symptoms within 60 days of injury, suggesting that mTBI can sensitize the cortex to the induction of CSD. To test this, we combined electrophysiology, neuroimaging, and behavioral assays in a mouse model of mTBI-induced PTH. After closed-head mTBI, injured mice exhibited a 160% increase in CSD induction probability (ie, lowered threshold) and became sensitized to CSD induction by brief exposure to stress, a common headache trigger. When evoked optogenetically, CSD produced prolonged periorbital and hind paw allodynia, consistent with headache-like pain. Subcutaneous onabotulinumtoxinA administered to the scalp after mTBI did not alter CSD susceptibility but completely abolished optogenetic CSD-induced allodynia. These findings suggest that mTBI elicits sensitization to CSD induction and promotes the emergence of aura in humans, likely contributing to PTH. It is important that, even after mTBI-induced sensitization, onabotulinumtoxinA decoupled CSD from pain behaviors, suggesting efficacy in treating PTH associated with aura.

items.title: Early codevelopment of pain, sleep disturbance, and hyperarousal after traumatic injury.
items.abstract: Chronic pain after traumatic injury likely reflects interacting processes rather than isolated recovery pathways, yet longitudinal evidence examining the joint development of pain, sleep disturbance, and hyperarousal from the acute postinjury stage is limited. We analysed data from the AURORA cohort of emergency department trauma survivors recruited within 72 hours of injury (n = 2834) to characterise trajectories of pain, sleep discontinuity, and hyperarousal over 12 months, identify shared multitrajectory profiles, and examine factors associated with adverse outcomes. Smartphone-based surveys assessed symptoms repeatedly from 1 to 5 days postinjury to one year. Group-based trajectory modelling identified 5 pain (n = 1635), 6 sleep discontinuity (n = 1635), and 5 hyperarousal (n = 1820) trajectories, ranging from rapid recovery to persistent high symptoms. Persistent high pain occurred in 35.1% of participants, while 23.5% followed persistently high or worsening sleep trajectories and 27.2% followed high hyperarousal trajectories. Multitrajectory modelling (n = 1800) identified 6 joint profiles, with 10.6% experiencing persistently high symptoms across all domains and 25.7% showing medium symptom levels. Older age and higher pretrauma pain were associated with adverse trajectories, whereas resilience and better prior mental health were protective. Baseline sleep discontinuity showed the strongest association with persistent high pain (adjusted odds ratio 3.31; 95% confidence interval 2.61-4.18), while physical activity was associated with a lower likelihood of medium-to-high pain trajectories. Female sex and lower income were associated with the most adverse multidomain profile. These findings highlight early postinjury sleep disruption, hyperarousal, and pain as interconnected processes. Targeting multiple domains may offer a promising strategy to prevent chronic pain after injury.

items.title: Temporal associations between pain intensity and disturbed body perception after total knee arthroplasty: a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model analysis.
items.abstract: Disturbed body perception is associated with chronic musculoskeletal pain, but its temporal relationship with pain after total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is unclear. We examined whether within-person fluctuations in knee-specific body perception are prospectively associated with pain intensity after TKA, beyond stable between-person differences. A total of 285 people undergoing primary TKA completed the Fremantle Knee Awareness Questionnaire (FreKAQ) and 100-mm visual analogue scales for pain during movement and resting pain preoperatively and at 1, 3, 6 months, and 1 year postoperatively. Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs) were estimated across 5 waves. Model fit was evaluated with the standardized root-mean-square residual (SRMR), comparative fit index (CFI), and root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA). Pain intensity and FreKAQ scores decreased over 1 year. In both RI-CLPMs, higher FreKAQ scores at 6 months were associated with greater pain intensity at 1 year (pain during movement: β = 0.262, P = 0.004; resting pain: β = 0.359, P = 0.003). Resting pain intensity at 3 months was associated with FreKAQ at 6 months (β = 0.179, P = 0.033), whereas no other paths from pain to subsequent FreKAQ scores were significant. Model fit was mixed, with acceptable SRMR and CFI values, but RMSEA values exceeding recommended thresholds. These results highlight a later recovery period warranting further assessment. Disturbed knee-specific body perception at 6 months may be associated with subsequent pain after TKA; however, these observational findings do not establish causality and warrant further longitudinal and interventional research before body-perception-focused rehabilitation can be recommended.

items.title: Noninvasive and objective near-real-time detection of pain changes during tonic fluctuating noxious heat stimulation.
items.abstract: Chronic pain involves natural intensity fluctuations that patients cannot control, contributing to learned helplessness and functional impairment. Detecting spontaneous pain decreases could enable precisely timed interventions that enhance perceived control. However, existing research on objective pain assessment has focused primarily on estimating static intensity from short, predictable stimuli rather than detecting moment-to-moment changes in ongoing pain. This study investigated whether pain decreases can be detected objectively using easily obtainable physiological signals during fluctuating pain. We recorded multiple physiological signals (8-channel electroencephalography, electrodermal activity, heart rate, pupil diameter, and facial expressions) from 42 healthy participants (mean age = 26.2 years, SD = 5.1) during calibrated tonic noxious heat stimulation on the left forearm with unpredictable intensity fluctuations (0-70 on visual analogue scale; twelve 3-minute trials). Temperature changes lasted 5 to 20 seconds. Using minimal preprocessing suitable for real-time applications, we trained deep learning models to classify pain decreases vs nondecreases from brief temporal windows, evaluated on a held-out test set (9 participants). Combining electrodermal activity, heart rate, and pupil diameter yielded optimal classification performance using a transformer-based architecture (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve = 0.854, accuracy = 76.8%). Electrodermal activity emerged as the most informative single predictor. Continuous stream analysis demonstrated median detection latency of 5.75 seconds with 70.4% sensitivity, reducible to 4.25 seconds at the cost of increased false positives. Results indicate that electrodermal activity and heart rate enable straightforward practical deployment, while highly variable signals such as electroencephalography and facial expressions require personalized fine-tuned models. These findings establish a basis for closed-loop interventions targeting spontaneous pain changes.

items.title: Perceived pleasantness mediates the effects of high-arousal and emotionally complex music on pain.
items.abstract: Music effectively reduces pain, yet the mechanisms underlying music-induced hypoalgesia remain poorly understood. We investigated how latent perceptual dimensions of music influence pain by examining both stimulus properties and subjective evaluations of those properties in 2 experiments. One hundred thirty-four participants listened to unfamiliar musical excerpts during thermal pain stimulation. Musical stimuli were systematically selected using the validated Arousal, Valence, Depth (AVD) model, which quantifies 3 key latent perceptual dimensions of music based on groups of descriptors such as "forceful" or "calming." Study A (n = 74) demonstrated that high arousal music increased pain unpleasantness, whereas high depth music provided relief, but crucially, these effects were completely mediated by participants' subjective ratings of musical pleasantness. Study B (n = 60) replicated the beneficial effect of musical depth and confirmed that participants' perceptions aligned with loadings of the AVD model dimensions. Individual differences in trait systemizing moderated the analgesic effect of depth in one study. Complete mediation by pleasantness ratings indicates that experiences of reward and subjective aesthetic evaluation, rather than perceived musical dimensions themselves, drives music-induced hypoalgesia. This suggests that musical pain interventions should prioritize deep and relaxing music that is well liked by the participant.

items.title: Association Between CTSG Variants and Persistent Postoperative Pain After Cardiac Surgery.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cathepsin G (CTSG) is a neutrophil-derived serine protease implicated in inflammatory pain modulation. Genetic variation in CTSG may influence postoperative pain susceptibility. This study evaluated the association between CTSG polymorphisms, CTSG plasma concentration and enzymatic activity, and long-term pain after cardiac surgery. METHODS: We conducted a prospective cohort study including 255 Caucasian adults undergoing elective cardiac surgery via median sternotomy. CTSG single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) rs2070697, rs2236742, and rs45567233 were genotyped. A random subsample of 107 patients underwent measurement of CTSG plasma concentration and enzymatic activity. Pain intensity (visual analogue scale [VAS]) at rest and with movement was assessed at 24 hours, 1 month, 6 months, and 12 months. Ordinal logistic regression was used to analyze associations between CTSG variants and pain. Mendelian randomization evaluated the causal effect of CTSG activity on pain. RESULTS: Overall, 16/250 patients (6.4%) reported moderate to severe postsurgical pain during movement at 6 months, and 6/178 patients (3.3%) at 12 months. At 1 month, pain was associated with higher BMI ( P = .016); at 12 months, it was more frequent in women ( P < .001) and in patients using antidepressants ( P = .022). The rs2070697 AA genotype was associated with reduced pain at 1 month at rest (GA vs AA: OR = 4.329, 95%CI = 1.523-12.310, P = .006), 6 months at rest and in movement (GA vs AA at rest: OR = 4.642, 95%CI = 1.535-14.040, P = .007; GA vs AA in movement: OR = 3.509, 95%CI = 1.169-10.530, P = .025), and 12 months in movement (GA vs AA: OR = 5.754, 95%CI: 1.492-22.200, P = .011). In contrast, the rs2236742 AA genotype was associated with increased pain at all three time points ( P < .05). Carriers of rs2236742 AA also reported greater preoperative informational anxiety (GG vs AA: OR = 0.193, 95%CI: 0.049-0.758, P = .018). CTSG activity was lower in rs2070697 A-allele carriers ( P = .03). CTSG activity and pain showed no causal association. No significant relationships were found for rs45567233. CONCLUSIONS: Variants appear to modulate susceptibility to prolonged post-sternotomy pain. These findings warrant validation in larger multi-ethnic cohorts to clarify mechanisms and potential implications for personalized perioperative pain management.

items.title: Immediate Perioperative Hypersensitivity and Anaphylaxis in Neuroanesthesia Practice: A Focused Review.
items.abstract: Perioperative hypersensitivity reactions are uncommon but potentially catastrophic. Neurosurgical and spine patients are especially vulnerable, as the injured brain and spinal cord tolerate anaphylaxis-induced hypotension poorly, cerebral and spinal perfusion may fall precipitously, and draping of the head and torso may obscure cutaneous signs. These procedures also rely heavily on topical hemostatic agents. National audits estimate the incidence of perioperative anaphylaxis at roughly 1 in 5000 to 10,000 anesthetics, but estimates vary geographically. No study has reported a denominator-based incidence confined to neurosurgery, leaving the true burden uncharacterized for this surgical specialty. This focused review summarizes the agents, mechanisms, and perioperative implications of immediate hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis relevant to neuroanesthesia. Immediate reactions are immunologic (IgE-mediated, or IgG- and complement-mediated) or nonimmunologic (direct mast-cell activation) but converge on mast-cell and basophil mediator release, which renders their presentations largely indistinguishable. We examine agents of relevance to neurosurgery, including neuromuscular blocking agents, cefazolin and other β-lactams, chlorhexidine, sugammadex, gelatin-based and other hemostatic agents, protamine, tranexamic acid, fluorescent and dye agents, and iodinated contrast media-alongside their mechanisms and safer alternatives. Management follows international consensus recommendations centered on prompt epinephrine administration and fluid resuscitation titrated to severity. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are useful adjuncts but should not delay resuscitation. Improved outcomes depend on greater awareness, careful allergy assessment and appropriate de-labeling, surgical-anesthesia communication, and wider access to testing and dedicated surveillance.

items.title: The role of central nervous system sensitization in obstetric pain: A focused review.
items.abstract: Obstetric pain conditions are clinically significant but often underrecognized complications of pregnancy and childbirth. Central nervous system sensitization (central sensitization) refers to the amplification of neural signaling in the central nervous system leading to pain hypersensitivity and offers a mechanistic framework for understanding acute and persistent obstetric pain. Central sensitization does not, however, act in isolation. It is initiated and sustained by ongoing input from sensitized peripheral nociceptors, potentially associated with pain amplification and persistence. This focused review synthesizes the neurophysiological mechanisms which may underlie sensitization in the peripartum period and examines the main obstetric pain conditions in which sensitization has been implicated, including pregnancy-related lumbopelvic pain, labor pain and persistent postpartum pain after vaginal delivery, persistent perineal pain, and chronic postcesarean pain. We also discuss psychological factors including anxiety, depression, pain catastrophizing, and fear of childbirth, as potential active modulators of central pain processing rather than merely coexisting conditions. These factors may represent modifiable targets for prevention, mitigation, and management. Key evidence gaps include the absence of obstetric-specific validation for clinical assessment tools such as the Central Sensitization Inventory, and limited prospective data linking intraprocedural nociception to postprocedural pain sensitization. Addressing these gaps through rigorously designed peripartum studies is essential for developing targeted, mechanism-based strategies to prevent and treat obstetric pain.

items.title: Ultrasound-guided genitofemoral nerve block for severe post-caesarean neuropathic pain: a case report.
items.abstract: Genitofemoral, ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric neuralgia are known complications of caesarean delivery. Diagnosis can be confirmed with selective low-volume nerve blocks. We present a case of a 37-year-old postpartum patient who developed intractable neuropathic pain immediately after caesarean delivery preventing mobility and discharge. A selective genitofemoral nerve block was performed using a vascular landmark technique due to obscuration of the round ligament by post-operative oedema. A perineural injection of bupivacaine, dexmedetomidine and dexamethasone resulted in 10 days of complete pain relief allowing for mobility and discharge. After 10 days, the pain returned, but at a manageable level allowing for outpatient management. A repeat block 42 days after caesarean delivery resulted in resolution of the neuropathic pain. This case demonstrates the use of vascular landmarks to accurately perform a low-volume diagnostic block during an acute post-operative pain crisis despite obscuring oedema.

items.title: Under pressure: lessons from and beyond entrapment neuropathies.
items.abstract: Entrapment neuropathies are the most prevalent focal neuropathic pain conditions globally and impose a substantial individual and socioeconomic burden. Traditionally conceptualised as purely mechanical compression syndromes, this view is increasingly challenged by converging evidence from human tissue analyses, advanced neuroimaging, and deep clinical phenotyping. Entrapment neuropathies are now recognised as biologically dynamic disorders shaped to different extents by microvascular compromise, demyelination, axonal degeneration, immune dysregulation, neuroinflammation, central nervous system adaptations, and psychosocial influences. Varying combinations and dominance of biopsychosocial processes give rise to marked clinical heterogeneity even within the same diagnostic label. This mechanistic diversity helps explain common diagnostic discordances, including extraterritorial symptom spread, normal electrodiagnostic findings despite clinical symptoms indicative of entrapment neuropathies, and imaging-clinical presentation mismatch. It also challenges one-size-fits-all treatment approaches, which have largely failed in entrapment neuropathies.Uniquely, entrapment neuropathies provide a natural human model of focal nerve injury in the context of neuropathic pain. Surgical decompression allows integration of tissue-level biology with precise clinical phenotypes and offers time-locked insights into recovery. Lessons derived from this model extend beyond entrapment neuropathies and can inform broader understanding of neuropathic and nerve-related musculoskeletal pain conditions. Here, we synthesise contemporary mechanistic insights, examine how biological heterogeneity translates into distinct clinical phenotypes, and discuss potential implications for mechanism-informed management.

items.title: Toward precision pediatric pain care: integrating mechanistic science, real-world measurement, and patient partnership.
items.abstract: Pediatric pain science is at an inflection point. Advances in neuroscience, behavioral science, digital health technologies, and patient engagement are rapidly expanding how chronic pain in youth can be understood, measured, and treated. Yet despite these advances, many children and adolescents continue to experience persistent pain-related disability and limited access to effective care, reflecting a gap between scientific discovery and real-world clinical practice. In this perspective, we propose the BRIDGE framework (Biobehavioral Research Integrated with Digital Monitoring and Guided Engagement) as a model for advancing pediatric pain research and care. Mechanistic science is increasingly identifying neural, behavioral, and contextual processes that contribute to pain persistence and recovery, creating opportunities to target modifiable mechanisms underlying pain-related disability. At the same time, digital health technologies including wearable sensors and ecological momentary assessment enable continuous measurement of activity, physiology, and patient-reported experiences in daily life, offering new insights into the dynamic nature of pain and the potential to develop digital biomarkers of risk, recovery, and treatment response. Central to this framework is meaningful partnership with youth and families, ensuring that innovations in measurement and intervention remain aligned with patient priorities and lived experience. Integrating these domains can support precision behavioral interventions, adaptive treatment strategies, and scalable models of care that expand access to evidence-based pediatric pain treatment.

items.title: Molecular histochemical analysis of neuroplasticity-related gene expression in pain pathway.
items.abstract: I am deeply honored to receive the 2026 John Bonica Prize for distinguished lifetime achievement in the basic science of pain. Reflecting on 40 years of research, this review paper will summarize my key findings to date. For the past four decades, my research has focused on elucidating the molecular mechanisms of pain using animal models. By integrating morphological techniques with molecular biology, behavioral analysis, and electrophysiological recordings, I have sought to clarify how pain signals are modulated and sustained under chronic pain conditions. Since the early stages of my career, I have been particularly interested in the diverse molecular dynamics within pain pathways and their functional significance. This long-term research has been driven by the conviction that a detailed analysis of gene expression changes within pain pathways-particularly those associated with neuroplasticity-is essential to understanding the mechanisms underlying intractable pain. This review provides a comprehensive overview of our investigation into the molecular and cellular mechanisms of chronic pain, focusing on gene expression analyses related mainly to dorsal root ganglion and spinal cord plasticity, alongside historically significant contributions from the global pain research community. Finally, I will also discuss recent methodological advances and their applications, as well as the challenges and future directions facing basic pain research.

items.title: Advancing equitable pain care worldwide requires progress in low- and middle-income settings: priorities for practice, research, and policy.
items.abstract: Equitable, high-value pain care remains out of reach for many populations worldwide, particularly for people living in low- and middle-income countries and cultural minority groups in high-income settings. Despite carrying a disproportionate burden of chronic pain, these populations remain underrepresented in high-quality pain research, underserved by existing health systems, and constrained by social, political, environmental, and commercial determinants of health. The lack of locally generated evidence forces clinicians and policymakers to rely on externally produced research that may not translate to local cultural, linguistic, or health-system contexts. This invited viewpoint synthesizes key contributors to pain inequity-including limited prioritization of chronic pain in low- and middle-income countries, underdeveloped rehabilitation capacity, poor access to essential treatments, commercial exploitation, and misalignment between culturally shaped pain beliefs and Western-derived assessment and treatment models. I highlight opportunities to strengthen equity in clinical care through improved education of health professionals and the public, culturally and linguistically responsive assessment, and contextually adapted self-management and treatment strategies. Equitable research requires standardized collection of sociodemographic variables, deliberate inclusion of underrepresented groups, and global partnerships that avoid colonizing practices. I propose principles for fair and impactful North-South collaborations focused on co-creation of research agendas, shared leadership, sustainable capacity building, and transparent governance. Advancing equitable global pain care and research will require collective action from clinicians, researchers, institutions, policymakers, journals, funders, and communities. A coordinated shift toward culturally grounded, contextually adaptable, and ethically collaborative approaches is essential to meaningfully reduce global pain disparities and ensure all individuals benefit from scientific progress.

items.title: The neuropathic chameleon: we are hot on the scent.
items.abstract: A common chronic pain condition, neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory or neural tissue and is characterized by a combination of negative (eg, numbness) and positive (eg, burning pain) sensory symptoms that significantly affect the quality of life. Common comorbidities such as depression and sleep disruption contribute to a substantial disease burden, which is further exacerbated by the apparent lack of effective therapeutic options. Current treatment options frequently achieve only partial, insufficient pain relief or may be completely ineffective in a considerable number of patients. The development of new drugs has thus far achieved moderate success, with many clinical trials failing to meet their primary endpoints; thus, a substantial unmet clinical need persists. One reason for this therapeutic deadlock is the considerable heterogeneity of neuropathic pain, driven by diverse pathophysiological mechanisms that vary between patients regardless of the underlying disease etiology. Accordingly, reclassification efforts follow a mechanism-based approach that reflects pathophysiological pain generators rather than disease etiology. Although diagnosis remains anchored in lesion- or disease-based criteria and structured clinical assessment, treatment development increasingly benefits from mechanism-informed phenotyping. A priori stratification based on individual mechanisms may help identify treatment responders, but implementation requires surrogate markers, as no biomarkers for pain mechanisms currently exist. In this article, we discuss candidate predictive markers and surrogate markers, focusing on sensory symptoms and signs assessed through patient-reported outcome measures and sensory testing, and their integration into future clinical trials.

items.title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity.
items.abstract: Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive "sleeping" nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

items.title: Exercise therapy for chronic pain: an updated perspective on mesocorticolimbic system function.
items.abstract: Patients with chronic pain often experience behavioral issues linked to pain, depression, and other emotional disorders. These problems stem from dysfunction in the mesocorticolimbic system, and exercise offers a safe, accessible, and effective alternative. It not only reduces pain but also activates multiple neural pathways, helping restore normal function. First, in the periphery, exercise promotes the release of myokines, which are essential for the body-brain connection and influence neural activity. IGF-1, released from muscles during exercise, can cross the blood-brain barrier and affect the brain. IGF-1 specifically targets orexin neurons in the hypothalamus, which then stimulate dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area, triggering the reward system. Second, exercise can reshape neural circuits and restore mesocorticolimbic function, reducing chronic pain and related issues. We showed that exercise activates neurons in the basal nucleus of the amygdala that project to the nucleus accumbens, supporting patients' goal-directed behavior. Moreover, inhibiting GABAergic neurons in the central nucleus of the amygdala decreases freezing behavior. Third, chronic pain often leads to depression, mainly due to reduced activity of serotonin (5-HT) neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus, which impairs the brain's reward system. Exercise boosts activity of 5-HT neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus. Furthermore, exercise can modify gene expression through epigenetic mechanisms, leading to long-lasting improvements in brain function and behavior. Overall, exercise can restore brain function, helping individuals overcome chronic pain and lead healthier lives. These findings support exercise therapy as a key component of chronic pain management and suggest mesocorticolimbic mechanisms underlying its effects.

items.title: Advances in research on combination therapy for the management of pain.
items.abstract: Pharmacotherapy remains an important component of multidisciplinary, multimodal pain treatment. Based on a well-established understanding of multiple concurrent mechanisms of nociceptive transmission and modulation, the demonstrated potential for synergistic interactions of drug combinations seen in preclinical studies supports the hypothesis of superior analgesia, and possibly also, fewer side-effects as compared with monotherapy. Likely related to this hypothesis and rationale, real-world evidence shows that approximately half of all patients with chronic pain, and even more with acute pain, concurrently receive 2 or more drugs from different mechanistic classes. To date, many dozens of randomized controlled trials have evaluated various analgesic combinations for the treatment of postoperative, neuropathic, back, arthritis, fibromyalgia, pelvic, and cancer-related pain conditions. Despite this growing area of research, most analgesic drug combinations are currently administered without rigorous evidence, thus exposing patients to the added cost or risk of some combinations that are not necessarily superior to monotherapy. As such, we propose future efforts to more efficiently exploit the potential benefits of combination therapy including: (1) expansion and coordination of translational collaborations to prioritize the most beneficial and clinically relevant combinations; (2) ensuring that preclinical combination studies evaluate multiple drug dosages and multiple relevant adverse effects; (3) ensuring that clinical trials include comparisons with each and every monotherapy component of the combination; (4) conducting further real-world studies of clinically beneficial combinations to ensure safety and efficacy in broader clinical settings; and (5) the application of these principles also to the evaluation of nonpharmacological treatment combinations.

items.title: Spontaneous neuropathic pain.
items.abstract: Spontaneous pain is a highly prevalent and disabling consequence of neuropathic disorders, yet it remains mechanistically underdefined and therapeutically underserved. Historically, preclinical animal models and clinical trials have been overwhelmingly biased toward stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity, relegating spontaneous pain to a secondary manifestation. Emerging evidence now challenges this view. Converging data from pharmacology, neural recordings, and systems-level causal manipulations indicate that spontaneous and stimulus-evoked pain arise from substantially dissociable molecular, cellular, and circuit substrates. Injured-fiber-derived ectopic activity within specific sensory neuron subtypes serves as a dominant peripheral generator of spontaneous pain, whereas cellularly distinct, intact spared-fiber pathways mediate stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity. At spinal and supraspinal levels, spontaneous pain preferentially engages affective-salience networks during pain chronification and may ultimately become stabilized within higher-order circuitry-while remaining dynamically coupled to afferent input. This mechanistic delineation carries critical translational implications. Current diagnostic and treatment guidelines rarely differentiate symptom domains, and most therapies have been validated primarily using stimulus-evoked or overall pain intensity endpoints-potentially contributing to a mechanism-therapy mismatch and variable efficacy. We argue that spontaneous neuropathic pain should be defined as a separate symptom domain rather than considered as a spontaneous manifestation of evoked pain mechanisms. This recognition demands longitudinal, biomarker-informed phenotyping to capture its persistent and fluctuating nature, and thereby enable robust mechanistic dissection at peripheral, spinal, and cortical nodes. Reframing spontaneous neuropathic pain along these lines will provide a foundation for precision therapeutics that target defined cell types, specific molecular drivers, and maladaptive network states-enabling mechanism-based, symptom-aligned treatments.

items.title: Prediction and prevention of pain after surgery.
items.abstract: Postoperative pain is common and has substantial clinical consequences for patients, their families, and society. Acute pain is not the only problem: a meaningful subset of patients develops chronic postsurgical pain, which is associated with considerable functional and psychosocial burden. Because established chronic postsurgical pain is difficult to treat, prevention is a key clinical objective, but it depends on the early identification of vulnerable patients and timely mechanism-informed interventions. This review examines mechanisms of postsurgical pain, as well as the prediction and prevention of unfavorable outcomes, from a translational perspective that integrates clinical evidence with mechanistic insights from preclinical models. After briefly summarizing recent developments, we outline current challenges and argue that progress requires alignment of outcome constructs across species, rigorous selection and reporting of experimental models, and identification of shared intermediate phenotypes linking mechanisms to patient trajectories. We then summarize the perioperative risk architecture underlying the transition from acute to chronic postsurgical pain, focusing on bio-psycho-social patient-related and surgical factors. Because current risk assessment tools do not yet provide sufficiently precise, reliable, and generalizable prediction, we discuss emerging evidence, including biological signatures that may refine prediction and risk stratification. We further argue that risk emerges dynamically through interactions across pre-, intra- and postsurgical phases. Building on this multi-stage, interactive framework, we propose a strategy integrating bio-psycho-social factors into clinically relevant prognostic models. Finally, we outline how this may not only help identify patients at risk, but also support mechanism-based, personalized prevention in vulnerable patients.

items.title: Brain sites involved in endogenous analgesia.
items.abstract: Pain modulation is a fundamental survival mechanism that prioritises, shapes, and suppresses nociceptive inputs to optimise behaviour. Although acute pain signals potential or actual tissue damage, sustained pain can impair essential behaviours, necessitating modulatory circuits that dynamically regulate nociception according to context and motivational state. These systems are deeply conserved, embedded within primitive spinal and brainstem structures, and capable of powerful modulation independent of cortical input, although higher regions such as the prefrontal cortex can influence their function. Decades of work have sought to identify these core modulatory circuits to advance basic understanding and develop strategies for clinically meaningful hypoalgesia. More recently, dysfunction within these circuits has been implicated in chronic pain, driving efforts to characterise how their organisation and function change during persistent pain states. Although most mechanistic insights come from animal studies, human neuroimaging, particularly since the advent of functional magnetic resonance imaging, has begun to map their location and engagement during pain modulation. Early work focused on forebrain regions due to the limited spatial resolution of standard MRI, but ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging now enables mm3-scale investigation of brainstem nuclei. This review synthesises evidence from animal and human studies to outline the best-characterised modulatory pathway, consisting of projections from the midbrain periaqueductal gray to the rostral ventromedial medulla and onward to the dorsal horn/spinal trigeminal nucleus, and highlights recent work detailing its organization.

items.title: Trustworthiness in pain research is essential. Developing and implementing the ENTRUST-PE framework.
items.abstract: Trustworthy pain research is essential for developing a deeper understanding of the phenomena, how it is experienced, its many impacts and how it might be reduced, prevented or managed to improve the lives of those who live with pain. Recognising multiple critical challenges that undermine trust in health research, an international, interdisciplinary network was convened to create an integrated framework for enhancing the trustworthiness of research in pain. The ENTRUST-PE framework was launched in 2024 with a call to action, proposing that trustworthiness in pain research is multidimensional and underpinned by 7 Core Values: Integrity and Governance; Equity, Diversity and Inclusivity; Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement; Methodological Rigour; Openness and Transparency; Balanced Communication and Data Authenticity. The framework includes specific recommendations for a range of interest holders and resources to support those recommendations. In this paper, we summarise the framework, reflect on the response to the framework from the pain research community, consider challenges and opportunities in the evolving research landscape and suggest how we might move towards deeper implementation to enhance the trustworthiness of pain research.

items.title: Chloride dysregulation: the next target for chronic pain therapeutics.
items.abstract: Chronic pain affects a substantial fraction of the population, yet pharmacological management remains deeply inadequate. This failure likely reflects the focus on developing analgesics suppressing normal nociceptive signalling rather than correcting the pathological substrates distinguishing chronic from acute pain. Here we review how the identification of injury-induced downregulation of the potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 in spinal dorsal horn neurons represents a landmark. It first provided a mechanistic, long-term substrate for spinal inhibitory failure. This form of disinhibition had the potential to explain several cardinal symptoms of neuropathic pain; not just hyperalgesia, through spinal hyperexcitability, and tactile allodynia, through cross-talk between sensory modalities, but also spontaneous pain, through enabling spontaneous bursts of activity in spinal nociceptive output to emerge. A second landmark is that chloride dysregulation as a substrate of disinhibition yields non-linear, non-intuitive predictions of neural circuit behaviours that shed light on several features of chronic pain and its therapeutic challenges. One is paradoxical pro-excitatory actions of tapping into normally endogenous inhibitory neurotransmission, potentially explaining failures of benzodiazepines analgesia and of conditional pain modulation. Others include degradation of sensory processing, possibly explaining diffuse pain, and leaky plasticity, predisposing to catastrophic sensitization. In turn, mechanisms regulating KCC2 itself emerge as substrates of chronification, as well as substrates of opioid-induced maladaptive paradoxical hyperalgesia. Finally, divergent yet convergent signaling cascades underlying KCC2-downregulation reveal a form of pathway degeneracy across sexes with lessons for therapeutics. All-in-all, these findings position KCC2 as a key novel target, not just for analgesia, but also for disease modification.

items.title: Pain as a predictive process in the brain: how the Bayesian brain generates, amplifies, and relieves pain.
items.abstract: Pain is not a passive readout of nociceptor traffic; it reflects the brain's inference about bodily threat under uncertainty. Building on predictive processing, active inference, and the free energy principle, we frame acute, chronic, and phantom pain as regimes of hierarchical inference in which memory, affect, and context shift the relative influence of prior beliefs vs incoming nociceptive evidence. Prior work links expectations to pain, but translating these ideas into a clinically usable account that links expectation mechanisms to measurable proxies of belief updating and to principled routes for personalized intervention remains challenging. We propose a generative model that links inferred threat to action policies, so that pain intensity and pain behavior can be studied within the same inferential loop. Within this framework, chronic pain can persist when threat beliefs remain overly influential despite corrective evidence. Placebo/nocebo effects illustrate how shifting expectations can amplify or relieve pain. Phantom pain illustrates how stable body-related beliefs can sustain pain-like perception even with minimal or absent afferent input. We outline candidate measurements and falsifiable predictions by linking expectation- and precision-related effects to a cingulate-insula-centered hub and associated descending control circuitry (periaqueductal gray to spinal dorsal horn). This account suggests principles for selecting and sequencing treatments to target belief content (expectations), evidence (corrective sampling), and gain control (context and neuromodulation), for matching mechanisms to patient-specific phenotypes, and for stratifying patients by dominant mechanism (overly threat-biased beliefs, reduced corrective sampling, or biased precision/gain control) to enable more testable trials and clearer interpretation of treatment response.

items.title: Pharmacological modulation of peripheral nerve excitability: a novel way to investigate sodium channel subtypes in humans.
items.abstract: Despite considerable progress in pain management, recommended systemic pharmacotherapy often comes with a high risk of serious side effects adversely affecting quality of life. Hence, topical routes of drug administration are currently gaining popularity in painful conditions such as diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) are expressed in peripheral nerves and are crucial for development and maintenance of neuropathic pain. Subtypes Nav1.7, 1.8, and 1.9 are highly expressed in nociceptors and are therefore interesting targets for topical pharmacotherapeutics. The aim of this study was to assess pharmacologically modulated excitability of peripheral sensory nerves using the human experimental perception threshold tracking technique, an indirect method for measuring the excitability of peripheral nerves. This randomized, placebo-controlled, and double-blinded study included 20 healthy participants. A novel electrical stimulation protocol-the Sodium channel Excitability Nociceptor Testing protocol-was used to identify alterations in Nav1.7, 1.8, and 1.9 after applying 3 (5% lidocaine, 10% phenytoin, and 2% mepyramine) topical pharmacological drugs. There was a significant difference in the relative increase in the perception threshold after drug application between drugs ( P < 0.01) and between drugs and placebo ( P < 0.01), except for phenytoin ( P = 0.22). The computational model suggests that lidocaine and mepyramine caused different alterations of the Nav1.7, 1.8, and 1.9 currents. The Sodium channel Excitability Nociceptor Testing protocol can be used to investigate differential pharmacological alterations of specific Nav subtypes. This may lead to better insight of neurophysiological mechanisms of sensory afferents, forming the basis for targeted drug development, leading the way to stratified treatment regimens of peripheral pain.

items.title: From research to practice: adapting graded sensorimotor retraining for people with chronic low back pain.
items.abstract: Low back pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide, yet translation of evidence-based interventions into clinical practice remains limited. Graded sensorimotor retraining, also known as the RESOLVE program, is a complex rehabilitation intervention for people with chronic low back pain that demonstrated clinically meaningful and sustained benefits in a sham-controlled, randomised controlled trial. This study aimed to adapt the RESOLVE program for implementation into a pragmatic clinical practice setting. We conducted a two-stage adaptation study guided by established frameworks. Stage 1 involved formation of an adaptation working group, review of evidence relevant to the RESOLVE program, qualitative interest-holder engagement, and ad hoc expert consultation. Findings from Stage 1 were used to identify core and adaptable components of the intervention and contextual determinants of implementation. Adaptations (or implementation strategies) to address the adaptable intervention components and contextual determinants were proposed to a consensus group meeting during Stage 2. During this stage, a structured consensus process finalised 8 adaptations, which target intervention content, delivery, resources, and clinician training. The adaptations focus on refining and streamlining existing components to improve fit rather than removing or introducing entire new elements. Our approach provides practical guidance for future adaptations of the RESOLVE program, and other complex treatments, for clinical implementation to ultimately improve the translation of evidence-based interventions for improved patient outcomes.

items.title: EEG-Guided Sevoflurane Anesthesia and Emergence Delirium in Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In pediatric anesthesia, minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) guides inhalational agent dosing but may not accurately reflect anesthetic depth. EEG-guided anesthesia has shown benefits in adults but remains underused in children. AIMS: This study aims to evaluate the effect of EEG-guided anesthesia with SedLine on emergence delirium (ED) and sevoflurane dose in behaviorally noncompliant children undergoing dental procedures under general anesthesia. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized controlled trial, 100 children aged 4-10 years were randomized to standard anesthesia guided by MAC and conventional clinical signs (standard group) or EEG-guided anesthesia titrated to SedLine parameters (primary target: PSI 25-50; secondary parameter: SEF 10-15 Hz) (EEG-S group). Primary outcome was ED incidence assessed by the Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium Scale (PAEDS). Secondary outcomes included mean EtSevo values, postoperative pain, rescue analgesia, nausea/vomiting, recovery time. RESULTS: Median PAEDS scores during the first 120 min postoperatively were significantly lower in the EEG-S group compared with the Standard group (e.g., upon arrival to PACU: 4 [IQR 4] vs. 8 [IQR 4.5]). In addition, the incidence of ED upon arrival in the recovery room was significantly lower in the EEG-S group (17% vs. 43%) and at 10 min postoperatively (17% vs. 37%). The mean end-tidal sevoflurane concentration was statistically lower in the EEG-S group (maintenance EtSevo 1.88 ± 0.25 vs. 1.98 ± 0.20; mean difference = 0.10, 95% confidence interval: 0.006-0.190; p = 0.036). Postoperative FLACC pain scores were also lower in the EEG-S group, representing a potential confounding factor for ED outcomes. CONCLUSION: EEG-guided anesthesia was associated with lower PAEDS scores and reduced sevoflurane consumption compared with standard management. However, given small EEG-derived differences and potential confounding by postoperative pain, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Within the applied target ranges, EEG-derived parameters were not independently associated with ED, and specific EEG targets predictive of ED could not be identified. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was registered (Protocol Registration Receipt NCT06400706/OKocaturk/May 02 2024) at http://www. CLINICALTRIAL: gov.

items.title: Automated Versus Manual Endotracheal Tube Cuff Pressure Control in Mechanically Ventilated Children: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Optimal endotracheal tube cuff pressure is key for airway sealing and minimizing microaspiration and tracheal injury in ventilated children. However, intermittent manual monitoring can allow significant pressure changes and be affected by measurement artifacts, potentially reducing airway protection. AIMS: This study evaluated whether automated cuff pressure control better maintains target pressure than manual monitoring in ventilated children, and assessed its effects on off-target pressure and workload. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized crossover study, mechanically ventilated pediatric patients (1 month-18 years) expected to require ventilation for ≥ 48 h underwent two randomized 24-h monitoring phases (manual and automated). During the manual phase, cuff pressure was continuously displayed via a closed system without repeated disconnection of the manometer and was intermittently adjusted by bedside nurses according to a predefined protocol. During the automated phase, cuff pressure was continuously regulated using an automated control system to maintain a target range of 15-25 cmH2O. The primary outcomes were the frequency and cumulative duration of off-target cuff pressure exposure; secondary outcomes included nursing workload. RESULTS: Thirty-two patients completed both phases (768 measurements). Low cuff pressure episodes (< 15 cmH2O) were more frequent during manual monitoring than automated monitoring (12.7% vs. 1.3%, p < 0.001), while high-pressure episodes (> 25 cmH2O) occurred only during manual monitoring (2.6% vs. 0%, p < 0.001). Total time outside the target range was markedly reduced with automated monitoring (118 vs. 10 h, p < 0.001). Nursing workload was significantly lower in the automated phase (3.65 h vs. 0.08 h, p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Automated cuff pressure control more reliably maintains target pressure and minimizes clinically important deviations compared to manual management. These results support adopting continuous automated regulation as a preferred strategy to enhance airway safety and reduce workload in mechanically ventilated children. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06965400).

items.title: Sugammadex versus neostigmine for neuromuscular blockade reversal in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reversal of neuromuscular blockade (NMB) is a routine component of general anaesthesia with important implications for recovery quality and peri-operative safety. Recent changes in the cost of sugammadex, together with its efficacy and adverse effect profile relative to neostigmine, may influence its broader clinical use. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of sugammadex compared with neostigmine in adult patients. DESIGN: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials with meta-analyses and trial sequential analyses. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. This is an update of a 2017 Cochrane review. DATA SOURCES: Online databases were searched up to December 2025. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Randomised trials enrolling adults receiving rocuronium or vecuronium for elective procedures and comparing sugammadex with neostigmine were included. The outcomes included NMB recovery time and risk of various adverse events. RESULTS: We included 165 trials with 19 124 participants. Risk of bias was generally unclear or high. NMB monitoring technique was reported in 113 trials, mostly acceleromyography. Time to reversal of NMB from second twitch to a train-of-four ratio more than 0.9 was shorter with sugammadex 2 mg kg-1 versus neostigmine 0.05 mg kg-1 (mean difference = -10.49 min (95% confidence interval, -11.90 to -9.08), GRADE: moderate). Sugammadex probably reduces the number of patients with at least one adverse event compared with neostigmine (risk ratio = 0.72 (95% confidence interval, 0.61 to 0.84), GRADE: moderate). When looking at specific adverse events, sugammadex probably reduces the risk of residual NMB, inadequate NMB reversal, desaturation, atelectasis, increased upper airway secretion, airway obstruction, bradycardia, dry mouth and urinary retention (GRADE: moderate). CONCLUSIONS: Sugammadex probably reverses NMB more rapidly and with fewer adverse events than neostigmine. Broader use of sugammadex has the potential to improve peri-operative outcomes.

items.title: Pre-Extubation Low-Dose Propofol in Pediatric Ear, Nose, and Throat Procedures: A Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-extubation emergence agitation (EA) is common in pediatric ear, nose, and throat (ENT) procedures and may lead to serious complications. AIMS: To assess the efficacy of low-dose propofol administered before extubation, compared with placebo, for preventing EA, using meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA). METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing low-dose propofol versus placebo administered before extubation in pediatric ENT procedures. The primary outcomes were laryngospasm, severity of EA, assessed by the Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium (PAED) scale score, and incidence of EA. Secondary outcomes included post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay, time to recovery, and time to extubation. Random-effects models were used to pool effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). TSA was performed for all outcomes to assess the robustness of the evidence. RESULTS: Ten RCTs were included in the review, of which six (414 pediatric patients) contributed to the meta-analysis. Compared with control, propofol significantly reduced the incidence of EA (risk ratio [RR] = 0.57; 95% CI, 0.42-0.78) and lowered agitation severity (mean difference [MD] = -3.94; 95% CI, -5.74 to -2.13). Time to extubation was slightly longer (MD = 1.8 min; 95% CI, 1.4-2.3), whereas time to recovery (MD = 0.9 min; 95% CI, -1.9 to 3.6) and PACU length of stay (MD = -0.63 min; 95% CI, -3.2 to 1.9) did not differ. TSA confirmed the robustness of the findings for incidence of EA, severity of EA, and time to extubation. However, the certainty of evidence was very low for severity of EA and moderate for EA incidence and time to extubation. Laryngospasm outcomes were not pooled due to substantial heterogeneity. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that pre-extubation propofol probably reduces the incidence of EA in pediatric ENT surgery, supported by moderate-certainty evidence, and may lower EA severity measured by PAED scale scores, for which the certainty of evidence was very low. Propofol was also associated with a slightly longer time to extubation, with no difference in overall recovery time or PACU length of stay.

items.title: Effects of Esketamine on Emergence Delirium in Children Undergoing Sevoflurane Anesthesia: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Trial Sequential Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Emergence delirium is a frequent and distressing postoperative complication in children, particularly following sevoflurane-based anesthesia. Despite its clinical importance, the optimal preventive strategy remains under investigation. This study aims to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of esketamine in preventing emergence delirium in pediatric patients undergoing sevoflurane-based general anesthesia. METHODS: We systematically searched seven databases and registries through 27 March 2026. Randomized controlled trials that compared esketamine with placebo in children undergoing surgical procedures were included. The primary outcome was the incidence of emergence delirium. Secondary outcomes were postoperative pain scores, extubation time, post-anesthesia care unit stay, and postoperative nausea and vomiting. Data were synthesized using random-effects models, with risk ratios for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences or standardized mean differences for continuous outcomes. Meta-regression and trial sequential analysis were performed. The risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials, and the certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach. RESULTS: Eight randomized controlled trials involving 916 patients were included. Esketamine significantly reduced the incidence of emergence delirium versus placebo (risk ratio = 0.35; 95% confidence interval: 0.26-0.48; p < 0.0001). No significant differences were observed between dosing regimens, surgical types, routes of administration, or timing of administration. Pain scores were significantly lower with esketamine (standardized mean difference = -0.58; 95% confidence interval: -0.79 to -0.37; p < 0.0001). Extubation time was modestly prolonged (mean difference = 1.72 min; 95% confidence interval: 0.20-3.24; p = 0.0267). Meta-regression revealed a statistically significant association between emergence delirium risk ratios and anesthesia duration (β = 0.98, p = 0.042), with no other significant associations observed for the other covariates. Post-anesthesia care unit stay showed no statistically significant difference, while postoperative nausea and vomiting was significantly reduced with esketamine (risk ratio = 0.69; 95% confidence interval: 0.49-0.97; p = 0.0304). items.title: As-needed inhaled corticosteroids in asthma: an Official American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing reliever therapy has demonstrated efficacy in improving asthma outcomes when compared to short-acting beta2-agonists (SABA) alone but remains underutilized. The purpose of this guideline is to provide recommendations surrounding the use of combination ICS-formoterol or ICS+SABA (in combination or separate inhalers) as reliever therapy across the asthma severity spectrum in adolescents and adults. METHODS: The American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline panel evaluated six research questions in the PICO format addressing the use of ICS-containing reliever therapy across National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) asthma treatment steps 1-5. The methodology team conducted systematic literature reviews and GRADE assessments, which the panel utilized to inform the recommendations for each specific PICO and overall. RECOMMENDATIONS: In patients at NAEPP steps 1 and 2, the panel made strong recommendations for the use of as-needed-only ICS-SABA or ICS-formoterol over SABA-only therapy, and conditional recommendations over scheduled ICS + as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5, the taskforce made a strong recommendation for the use of maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) with ICS-formoterol over scheduled ICS-LABA plus as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5 who are using scheduled maintenance ICS-LABA, the panel made a conditional recommendation for use of ICS+SABA reliever over SABA reliever. In considering these recommendations, the panel valued the importance of preventing severe exacerbations and considered the risk of SABA-only treatment, as well as ICS and systemic corticosteroid (SCS) exposure. CONCLUSIONS: This clinical practice guideline, informed by systematic reviews and GRADE-based appraisals of PICO-framed evidence, makes these evidence-based recommendations for the safe and effective use of ICS-containing reliever therapy in asthma.

items.title: Comparing Subglottic Ultrasound and Distal Phalanx Width for Pediatric Endotracheal Tube Sizing in a Predominantly School-Aged Pediatric Cohort: A Prospective Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate endotracheal tube (ETT) sizing is essential in pediatric airway management to optimize ventilation and reduce complications. Traditional methods, including age-based formulas and distal phalanx width (DPW), may lack precision. Subglottic ultrasound (US) has emerged as a promising tool, but its predictive accuracy compared with DPW remains unclear. This study aimed to compare accuracy, agreement, diagnostic performance, and clinical applicability of subglottic US versus DPW for predicting optimal ETT size in children, while recognizing that the enrolled cohort was predominantly school-aged. METHODS: In this prospective observational study, pediatric patients aged 0-12 years undergoing elective or emergency intubation were assessed. Pre-intubation measurements included subglottic transverse airway diameter by ultrasound (ACUSON Juniper, microconvex probe, 5-10 MHz) and DPW by digital calipers. Predicted ETT sizes were compared with the final clinically accepted cuffed ETT inner diameter confirmed by leak testing and cuff pressure optimization. Agreement was evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients, while diagnostic performance was defined a priori as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), likelihood ratios, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Logistic regression identified predictors of good ETT fit. RESULTS: Among 160 patients, the median age was 8.8 years (IQR 7.0-10.5), indicating predominance of older children. Ultrasound-predicted ETT size showed a stronger correlation with actual size (r = 0.479, p < 0.001) than DPW (r = 0.248, p = 0.002). Ultrasound predictions had narrower Bland-Altman limits of agreement, although ultrasound measurement is operator-dependent. DPW showed poor sensitivity (5.9%) but high specificity (99.3%) for identifying underfit ETTs, with limited overall discrimination (ROC AUC = 0.53). Only subglottic diameter was a significant predictor of good ETT fit. CONCLUSION: Subglottic ultrasound showed better agreement with clinically accepted ETT size than DPW in this predominantly school-aged pediatric cohort. These findings support the potential role of ultrasound as an adjunct to pediatric airway assessment, but conclusions should be interpreted cautiously in infants and younger children because they were under-represented. Standardized measurement protocols and operator training are needed

items.title: The Association Between Intraoperative Cell Salvage and Tumor Recurrence in Patients Undergoing Meningioma Resection: An Observational Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The oncologic safety of intraoperative cell salvage (ICS) during meningioma surgery remains controversial due to concerns about hematogenous tumor dissemination. We investigated the association between ICS use and postoperative tumor recurrence in patients undergoing meningioma resection. METHODS: This study retrospectively included adult patients who underwent meningioma resection with intraoperative blood loss >1000 mL at Beijing Tiantan Hospital between August 2015 and November 2022. The primary outcome was postoperative tumor recurrence. Propensity scores were estimated using clinically relevant baseline variables, and inverse probability of treatment weighting with stabilized weights was applied to reduce confounding. RESULTS: Among 988 patients, 89 (9.0%) developed recurrence during a mean follow-up of 60 months. Recurrence was less frequent in patients receiving ICS than in those without ICS (7.9% vs. 14.9%, P=0.004). After inverse probability of treatment weighting adjustment, baseline characteristics were well balanced between groups. In the weighted Cox model, ICS use was not associated with increased recurrence risk (HR=0.62, 95% CI: 0.39-0.99, P=0.043). Higher WHO grade was independently associated with increased recurrence risk, whereas gross total resection was associated with reduced risk. Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent results. CONCLUSION: In patients undergoing meningioma surgery with substantial intraoperative blood loss, intraoperative cell salvage was not associated with an increased risk of tumor recurrence.

items.title: A Pilot and Feasibility Study of a Four-Stage Neurological Staging Framework in Pediatric Tracheal Extubation During Anesthesia Emergence.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative tracheal extubation is a particularly high-risk period in pediatric anesthesia. Because emergence from anesthesia is a complex and complicated process, determining the optimal timing for safe tracheal extubation remains challenging. AIMS: To evaluate the feasibility and descriptive characteristics of a four-stage neuroanatomical framework for pediatric anesthesia emergence while providing exploratory incidence estimates of respiratory adverse events across these stages. METHODS: Children younger than 7 years undergoing general anesthesia were enrolled. Emergence stratified into four stages, defined by cranial nerve indicators: Stage 1 (Medulla: regular breathing, movement, excluding cough or swallowing); Stage 2 (Pons: tearing or grimacing); Stage 3 (Midbrain: conjugate gaze or eye-opening); and Stage 4 (Cerebrum: purposeful movement). Primary outcomes included feasibility metrics-such as protocol completion, recruitment flow, and data completeness-and successful assignment of emergence stages. Exploratory descriptive statistics summarized the incidence of respiratory adverse events. Risk ratios were calculated to compare the occurrence of respiratory adverse events in intermediate (Stages 2 and 3) and cortical (Stage 4) stages. RESULTS: Of the 174 patients screened, 89 completed the protocol. Overall, 153 patients provided consent (91.6% consent rate). The overall data capture rate was 58.2% (89/153), while the worksheet processing rate-adjusted for protocol-ineligible cases, such as those with supraglottic airway use-was 73.2% (112/153). Among the 89 patients analyzed, there were no missing data for key variables, and stage assignment was achieved in all cases. Respiratory adverse events were observed in 16.9% of children; descriptive analysis showed an event rate of 25.0% during Stage 2, 25.0% during Stage 3, and 11.6% during Stage 4. CONCLUSIONS: While stage assignment was possible among captured cases, the predefined data capture targets were not met. This pilot study successfully identified key workflow and feasibility barriers, which establish a foundation for refining protocols in the upcoming multicenter ExPEDIA registry. items.title: Sugammadex interference with serum progesterone measurement: an in-vitro study.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Sugammadex may interfere with serum progesterone immunoassays, potentially rendering measured concentrations and resulting recommendations unreliable. METHODS: We investigated the effect of a range of sugammadex concentrations on serum progesterone concentrations in samples from pre-menopausal female volunteers. Samples were spiked with sugammadex concentrations (15-120 μM), corresponding to clinical doses between 2 mg.kg-1 and 19 mg.kg-1. Total progesterone concentrations in each sample were determined using the routine electrochemiluminescence immunoassay method. A subgroup of 15 samples underwent further testing using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectroscopy, comparing baseline with sugammadex 120 μM. RESULTS: Thirty-five participants provided blood samples. Increasing concentrations of sugammadex were associated with lower measured serum progesterone, with an approximate 10% reduction with each doubling of sugammadex concentration (F(2,30) = 4.86, p = 0.015). Overall, progesterone concentrations decreased by a mean (SD) of 34.6% (12.4%) between control samples and those spiked with sugammadex 120 μM (p = 0.015). In contrast, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectroscopy showed no statistically significant biochemical change in progesterone concentrations between baseline and sugammadex 120 μM. DISCUSSION: Sugammadex produced a dose-dependent reduction in the progesterone concentrations when measured by immunoassay techniques, but not by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectroscopy. This suggests that an immunoassay interference occurs across clinically relevant doses. Progesterone results from routine laboratory testing should be interpreted with caution in the presence of sugammadex. WHAT WE DID: We studied blood samples from 35 women to see whether a medicine called sugammadex affects progesterone test results. We added different amounts of sugammadex to the samples and then measured progesterone levels using a common hospital laboratory test. We also checked some samples using a second, more precise testing method. WHY DID WE DO IT: Progesterone is an important hormone, and doctors sometimes measure it to make decisions about a patient's health.
